key_instruments: EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689)
scope: all AI systems, with a risk-based tiering (banned practices, high-risk, limited-risk transparency duties, general-purpose AI models); binding across all 27 EU member states
enforcement_mechanism: yes — national market-surveillance authorities plus a new EU AI Office; fines up to 7% of global annual revenue (or €35m) for banned-practice violations, up to 3% for other breaches
effective_date_or_status: Entered into force 1 Aug 2024; banned practices + AI literacy rules applied from 2 Feb 2025; general-purpose AI model rules from 2 Aug 2025; most other rules (incl. enforcement/penalties) from 2 Aug 2026; high-risk system rules from 2 Dec 2027 (an 'AI Digital Omnibus' package agreed May 2026 pushed some high-risk deadlines back further)
plain_language_summary: The EU is the first place in the world with a real, binding AI law. It bans a few dangerous uses of AI outright, and for 'high-risk' uses like hiring or credit-scoring tools, companies must test and register the systems before selling them. Fines for breaking the rules can reach 7% of a company's worldwide revenue. It's being rolled out in stages through 2027, and some deadlines were just pushed back in 2026.

key_instruments: OECD AI Principles (2019, updated May 2024)
scope: all AI systems; principles-level guidance for governments and companies, not enforceable rules
enforcement_mechanism: no — voluntary principles with no fines or licensing; OECD tracks country policies via the OECD.AI Policy Observatory but has no enforcement power
effective_date_or_status: Adopted 2019, substantively updated May 2024 to add generative AI, safety, and misinformation provisions; endorsed by 47 countries/jurisdictions as of the 2024 update
plain_language_summary: This is a shared set of values — like 'AI should be safe, fair, and transparent' — that 47 countries have agreed to aim for. It's not a law and nobody can be fined for ignoring it, but it shapes how many countries write their own AI rules.

key_instruments: Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law (CETS 225)
scope: AI systems used by public authorities and private actors, focused on human rights/democracy/rule-of-law impacts; open to non-European countries too
enforcement_mechanism: intended yes once in force (first-ever legally binding international AI treaty) — but not yet in force; each ratifying country sets its own enforcement/oversight body domestically
effective_date_or_status: Opened for signature 5 Sept 2024; needs 5 ratifications (incl. 3 Council of Europe member states) to enter into force; as of 7 Sept 2026 only the EU has ratified (15 May 2026) — not yet in force
plain_language_summary: This would be the world's first binding international AI treaty covering human rights, but it's stuck in the starting gate: countries have to formally ratify it before it counts, and so far (as of late 2026) only the EU itself has actually done so, even though over 20 countries including the UK, US, and Switzerland have signed on in principle.

key_instruments: UNGA Resolution on 'Seizing the opportunities of safe, secure and trustworthy AI' (March 2024); Global Digital Compact (Sept 2024, part of the Pact for the Future); UNGA Resolution A/RES/79/325 (Aug 2025) creating the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI and Global Dialogue on AI Governance; separate Dec 2024 resolution on military AI
scope: global, all AI systems at a high level — mostly institution-building and shared principles rather than rules for specific systems
enforcement_mechanism: no — these are UN resolutions and compacts with no binding force and no penalties; the new Scientific Panel produces research/assessments, not enforcement
effective_date_or_status: Resolutions adopted March 2024, Sept 2024, Dec 2024, and Aug 2025; the Scientific Panel and Global Dialogue on AI Governance are newly-established bodies as of 2025, still standing up
plain_language_summary: The UN has gotten nearly every country in the world to agree, on paper, that AI should be safe and beneficial, and has just set up a new expert panel and a global forum to study AI risks together. None of this creates enforceable rules — it's diplomacy and shared research, not law.

key_instruments: Hiroshima Process International Code of Conduct for Organisations Developing Advanced AI Systems (Oct 2023) + Comprehensive Policy Framework; OECD-run reporting framework launched Feb 2025
scope: advanced/frontier general-purpose AI systems developed by large AI companies, not AI generally
enforcement_mechanism: no legal enforcement — voluntary code of conduct; companies self-report against it via an OECD-hosted monitoring framework (first reports due April 2025)
effective_date_or_status: Code of Conduct agreed and endorsed by G7 leaders Oct-Dec 2023; carried forward under Italy's 2024 G7 presidency; OECD monitoring/reporting framework went live Feb 2025 with rolling company reports
plain_language_summary: The G7 countries got major AI companies to voluntarily sign a code of good conduct for their most powerful AI systems and to self-report on how they're following it. There's no fine or punishment if a company doesn't comply — it relies on public pressure and peer tracking.

key_instruments: ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics (Feb 2024) + Expanded ASEAN Guide on AI Governance and Ethics — Generative AI (Jan 2025)
scope: all AI systems at a regional guidance level, with a generative-AI-specific expansion; applies across ASEAN's 10 member states as voluntary guidance, not a bloc-wide law
enforcement_mechanism: no — voluntary guide; individual ASEAN member states (e.g. Singapore) may separately have their own binding or non-binding rules, tracked in their own country rows
effective_date_or_status: Original guide issued Feb 2024; expanded generative-AI version issued Jan 2025
plain_language_summary: Southeast Asia's 10 countries agreed on a shared voluntary rulebook for trustworthy AI, covering things like fairness and privacy, and later added extra guidance specifically for generative AI (like ChatGPT-style tools). It's a recommended playbook, not an enforceable law, and each country can still make its own separate rules.

key_instruments: Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy
scope: all AI systems, continent-wide strategic guidance for AU's 55 member states — sets shared goals, not enforceable rules; implementation is left to individual countries
enforcement_mechanism: no — a strategy document, not a law; AU has no power to fine or license; enforcement (if any) would come from individual member states adopting their own laws
effective_date_or_status: Endorsed by the AU Executive Council 18-19 July 2024 in Accra, Ghana
plain_language_summary: African Union countries agreed on a shared game plan for developing AI in ways that benefit Africa — building skills, attracting investment, and managing risks — but this is a strategic roadmap, not a law, and each of the 55 member countries decides its own actual rules (most currently have none, see individual country rows).

region_or_country: Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) / Bletchley Declaration & AI Safety Summit process
key_instruments: Bletchley Declaration (Nov 2023, signed by 28 countries + EU); follow-on Seoul (2024) and Paris (2025) AI Safety Summits; Global Partnership on AI, which merged into the OECD in 2024
scope: advanced/'frontier' AI systems and general international AI-safety cooperation; not a comprehensive rulebook for everyday AI use
enforcement_mechanism: no — declarations and summit commitments with no fines or licensing; produced some shared outputs (e.g. a network of national AI Safety Institutes) but no binding enforcement
effective_date_or_status: Bletchley Declaration signed Nov 2023; Seoul Summit May 2024; Paris AI Action Summit Feb 2025; next GPAI Summit scheduled Bratislava, Slovakia, Nov 2025; GPAI formally merged into the OECD in 2024
plain_language_summary: This is a running series of international summits (UK, South Korea, France, and more to come) where countries agree, in writing, to cooperate on the risks of the most powerful 'frontier' AI models. It has produced shared statements and a network of AI safety research institutes, but no binding rules or penalties.

key_instruments: No comprehensive federal AI law; patchwork of binding state laws (Colorado AI Act, California AI transparency/employment laws, Illinois, Texas, Utah), sector-specific federal agency enforcement, and a Dec 2025 federal Executive Order ('Ensuring a National Policy Framework for Artificial Intelligence') aiming to preempt state laws
scope: varies hugely by state and sector — e.g. Colorado covers 'high-risk' AI used in consequential decisions (employment, credit, housing); California covers AI transparency and employment uses; no single law covers all AI nationally
enforcement_mechanism: yes at the state level in states with laws (state attorneys general enforcement, some private rights of action); federal enforcement is via existing agency authority (FTC, EEOC, etc.) applied to AI, not an AI-specific statute; a Dec 2025 federal executive order is trying to override/preempt state AI laws via a new DOJ litigation task force
effective_date_or_status: No comprehensive federal law as of Sept 2026; Colorado AI Act's replacement framework starts Jan 1, 2027; California AI Transparency Act operative Aug 2026; federal preemption executive order signed Dec 11, 2025, with legal fights over its validity ongoing
plain_language_summary: The US has no single national AI law. Instead, individual states like Colorado and California have passed their own binding rules — mostly about being transparent when AI is used in things like hiring or lending. In late 2025 the federal government tried to override those state laws with an executive order, and as of late 2026 that fight over who's in charge (states or the federal government) is still playing out in court.

key_instruments: No federal AI-specific statute (the proposed Artificial Intelligence and Data Act, AIDA, died when Parliament was prorogued Jan 2025 and will not return); governance instead comes from federal privacy law (PIPEDA), Quebec's Law 25 (binding rules on automated decision-making), a voluntary federal Code of Conduct for generative AI, and sector-specific directives (financial services, government procurement, health tech)
scope: privacy and automated-decision-making aspects of AI are covered by binding law (mainly in Quebec); generative AI development is covered only by a voluntary code; no general cross-sector binding AI statute
enforcement_mechanism: yes for the privacy-law pieces (Quebec's privacy regulator can investigate and fine under Law 25); no enforcement for the voluntary generative-AI Code of Conduct
effective_date_or_status: AIDA formally abandoned; federal government tabled Bill C-36 (privacy reform) June 15, 2026, which does not revive AIDA; Canada launched a $2B, 5-year 'AI for All' National AI Strategy June 4, 2026 (investment/policy package, not a binding law)
plain_language_summary: Canada tried to pass a big national AI law but it died in Parliament in 2025 and the government has said it isn't coming back. Right now AI in Canada is governed by a patchwork: Quebec has real, enforceable privacy rules that cover automated decisions, the federal government only has a voluntary 'be responsible' code for AI companies, and there's a big new government investment strategy — but no binding, all-of-Canada AI law.

key_instruments: Bill PL 2338/2023 ('Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial') — a comprehensive, EU-AI-Act-inspired risk-based framework
scope: would cover all AI systems with a risk-tiered approach (banned practices, high-risk obligations); includes contested provisions requiring payment for copyrighted training data
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — bill includes proposed oversight/liability mechanisms but has not been enacted, so nothing is enforceable yet
effective_date_or_status: Approved by the Senate Dec 10, 2024; as of May 2026 still under review by a special committee in the Chamber of Deputies (House), with additional related bills introduced as recently as Feb 2026; no enactment date yet
plain_language_summary: Brazil has written a detailed, EU-style AI law and its Senate already approved it back in 2024, but it's still stuck in the lower house of Congress being debated and amended — including a controversial rule that would require AI companies to pay for the copyrighted material they train on. It is not yet in effect.

key_instruments: National Law to Regulate the Use of Artificial Intelligence (Senate bill introduced Feb 11, 2026, by Sen. Karina Ruíz); plus a narrower April 2026 reform to labor and copyright law covering AI use of performers' image/voice
scope: the pending comprehensive bill would cover public- and private-sector AI broadly, including bans on things like AI-driven lethal autonomous weapons and electoral deepfakes; the enacted labor/copyright reform covers only performers' image and voice rights
enforcement_mechanism: the labor/copyright reform (enacted April 2026) is binding; the comprehensive AI bill is not yet law so has no enforcement yet
effective_date_or_status: Comprehensive bill introduced to the Senate Feb 11, 2026, referred to committee, anticipated for further discussion in the Sept 2026 session — no enactment as of research date; separate labor/copyright AI reform passed the Chamber of Deputies April 7, 2026
plain_language_summary: Mexico doesn't have a general AI law yet, despite over 100 attempts at bills since 2020. A serious new comprehensive bill was introduced to the Senate in February 2026 and could be debated further in September 2026. Separately, Mexico already passed a narrower, real law in April 2026 protecting performers' faces and voices from being copied by AI without consent.

key_instruments: Federal: 'Recommendations for Reliable Artificial Intelligence' (Provision 2/2023) — non-binding ethical guidelines for national public administration; plus binding but narrow provincial rules in 4 provinces (Buenos Aires, Jujuy, Río Negro, San Juan) on ethical use/human oversight in public and judicial AI use
scope: federal guidelines cover AI use across the national public sector as voluntary recommendations; provincial rules are binding but limited to public/judicial-sector AI in those 4 provinces only, not private-sector AI nationally
enforcement_mechanism: no enforcement at the federal level (voluntary guidelines); provincial rules may carry binding force within their sector/jurisdiction, but no comprehensive national enforcement regime exists
effective_date_or_status: Federal recommendations issued June 1, 2023; provincial regulations in place as of early 2026; a new bill on 'cognitive autonomy' protecting minors from AI profiling was introduced Feb 20, 2026 and remains pending
plain_language_summary: Argentina has no binding national AI law — just voluntary ethical guidance for its own government agencies. A handful of provinces have made their own binding rules, but only for AI used in public services and courts, not for AI in general. A new bill to protect children from AI profiling was introduced in 2026 but hasn't passed.

key_instruments: AI Regulation Bill (Boletín N° 16.821-19), introduced by the Presidency May 2024 — an EU-AI-Act-style, risk-tiered bill
scope: would cover all AI systems (including foreign providers whose AI outputs reach Chilean users), with a risk classification system, bans on unacceptable-risk uses, and synthetic-content/deepfake labeling rules
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — bill is still in the legislative process (second constitutional review in the Senate as of 2026); separately, Chile's new comprehensive data-protection law (Ley 21.719, GDPR-style) becomes enforceable Dec 1, 2026 and will interact with AI systems that process personal data
effective_date_or_status: AI bill introduced May 2024, in second constitutional review in the Senate as of 2025/2026, not yet enacted; related Ley 21.719 (data protection, not AI-specific) takes effect Dec 1, 2026
plain_language_summary: Chile is working on its own EU-style AI law that would classify AI systems by risk level and require labeling of deepfakes, but it's still moving through the Senate and isn't law yet. A separate, unrelated new privacy law (not AI-specific) does take effect at the end of 2026 and will affect any AI system that handles personal data.

key_instruments: Bill 025 of 2026 (before the House of Representatives) and Statutory Bill 154 of 2024 — both propose comprehensive AI regulation with risk/impact assessments, transparency, human oversight, and a high-risk-system registry
scope: would cover developers, providers and deployers of AI systems broadly, with extra duties for systems affecting fundamental rights; a narrower binding rule (Resolution 1644 of 2026) already governs AI use in telemedicine specifically
enforcement_mechanism: not yet for the general bills (not enacted); the telemedicine resolution is binding and requires that clinical decisions stay with human professionals, who can accept/modify/reject AI recommendations
effective_date_or_status: Bill 025 of 2026 pending in the House as of research date; Statutory Bill 154 pending since 2024; Ministry of Health Resolution 1644 of 2026 on telemedicine AI already in force
plain_language_summary: Colombia doesn't have a general AI law yet, but two comprehensive bills are moving through Congress that would require companies to assess and disclose AI risks. In the meantime, Colombia already has one narrow binding rule in place: AI can suggest things in telemedicine, but a human doctor always has the final say.

key_instruments: Law No. 31814 (Law promoting the use of AI for economic and social development) + its implementing regulation, Supreme Decree No. 115-2025-PCM
scope: applies broadly to AI development and use across public and private sectors, with obligations including impact assessments, human oversight, and technical documentation retention
enforcement_mechanism: yes — oversight from the Secretariat for Government and Digital Transformation (SGTD) and, for data-related aspects, the National Authority for Protection of Personal Data (ANPD); specific penalty amounts were not confirmed in this search and should be checked against the primary regulation text
effective_date_or_status: Law enacted 2023; implementing Supreme Decree published Sept 9, 2025; regulation entered into force Jan 22, 2026 (90 business days after publication); public-sector compliance deadline Sept 9, 2026; private-sector compliance phased over up to 4 years
plain_language_summary: Peru became the first country in Latin America with a real, general AI regulation now in force. Companies and government agencies using AI have to assess the risks, keep humans in the loop, and document what their systems do — government agencies had until September 2026 to comply, and private companies get up to 4 years to catch up. I could not confirm the exact fine amounts for breaking the rules, so that detail needs a follow-up check.

key_instruments: No AI-specific statute; 'pro-innovation' principles-based approach where existing sectoral regulators (FCA for finance, MHRA for medicines, Ofcom for media/telecoms) apply existing law (incl. UK GDPR and the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025) to AI within their remits; a narrow bill on powerful AI models was promised in July 2024 but never introduced; a new 'Regulating for Growth' Bill (mainly about regulatory sandboxes, not general AI rules) was announced in the 2026 King's Speech
scope: no single AI-specific scope — coverage depends on which existing sector regulator is involved and what existing law (data protection, consumer, financial services, medical devices) applies to a given AI use
enforcement_mechanism: enforcement exists but only through each sector regulator's existing (non-AI-specific) powers — e.g. the UK data protection regulator (ICO) can act under GDPR-derived law; there's no AI-specific fine or licensing regime
effective_date_or_status: No AI-specific bill in force or introduced to Parliament as of research date; the promised narrow AI-models bill has not materialized (as of July 2026 reports said 'no AI bill in the short-to-medium term'); Regulating for Growth Bill draft expected around Nov 2026, but may slip given a change in prime minister
plain_language_summary: The UK has deliberately chosen not to pass a general AI law. Instead, existing regulators — the ones that already oversee banks, medicines, and broadcasters — are expected to apply their existing powers to AI in their own sectors. A promised AI bill for the most powerful AI systems was announced back in 2024 but still hadn't been introduced to Parliament as of late 2026.

key_instruments: No AI-specific law yet; Federal Council adopted a regulatory-approach decision in early 2025 aiming to incorporate the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on AI into Swiss law; a bill is planned to be sent for consultation by end of 2026, alongside separate non-binding measures
scope: would primarily apply to state/public-sector actors first (per the Council of Europe Convention's initial focus), with transparency, data protection, non-discrimination and supervision as planned areas; private-sector AI currently governed only by general (non-AI-specific) law
enforcement_mechanism: no — nothing AI-specific is currently binding; enforcement would come once a bill is drafted, consulted on, and passed, which had not happened as of the research date
effective_date_or_status: Federal Council set the regulatory approach in early 2025; a draft bill for public consultation is planned by end of 2026; separately, non-legally-binding measures are also being drawn up by end of 2026 — nothing enacted yet
plain_language_summary: Switzerland doesn't have an AI law yet. The government decided in 2025 on a general direction — loosely following a Council of Europe treaty — and is planning to put an actual draft bill out for public comment by the end of 2026. Until then, AI in Switzerland is governed only by general laws that weren't written with AI in mind.

key_instruments: KI-loven (a dedicated Norwegian AI Act incorporating the EU AI Act, since Norway is in the EEA/European Economic Area but not the EU)
scope: would mirror the EU AI Act's risk-based scope (banned practices, high-risk system obligations, transparency rules) once in force, plus Norway-specific implementation details (e.g. national coordination via Nkom, a regulatory sandbox)
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — law needs to be incorporated into the EEA Agreement and passed by the Norwegian Parliament; sources conflict on exact status: some describe it as on track for summer/August 2026, others say the process 'has been delayed'
effective_date_or_status: Sent for public consultation June 2025; originally targeted to align with the EU's August 2026 timeline, but at least one August 2026 source describes the Norwegian law as delayed — exact in-force status as of Sept 2026 is unclear and needs a fresh primary-source check
plain_language_summary: Norway isn't in the EU but is adopting essentially the same AI rulebook as the EU, through its own national law. The plan was to have it in force around the same time as the EU (mid-2026), but the sources I found disagree on whether that actually happened on schedule or has slipped — this needs a fresh check to confirm whether Norway's AI Act is now actually in force.

key_instruments: Draft Artificial Intelligence Law Bill (2/2234), submitted to Parliament June 2024, EU-AI-Act-style risk classification — not yet enacted; in the meantime, Turkey's Data Protection Law (No. 6698, KVKK) Article 11(1)(g) gives people a right to object to fully-automated decisions, and the Turkish data protection authority (KVKK) has issued non-binding AI guidance (April 2025 recommendations, Nov 2025 generative-AI guide, March 2026 agentic-AI guidance)
scope: the pending bill would cover AI broadly with risk-tiered obligations; the currently-binding piece (Art. 11(1)(g) of the data protection law) only covers automated decisions affecting individuals, not AI generally
enforcement_mechanism: the data-protection-law provision is binding and enforceable by the KVKK; the AI-specific bill has no enforcement since it isn't law; the KVKK's AI guidance documents are explicitly non-binding
effective_date_or_status: Draft AI Law Bill submitted June 2024, not enacted as of July 2026; a broader 2026-2030 National AI Strategy is in preparation; KVKK guidance documents issued April 2025, Nov 2025, and March 2026
plain_language_summary: Turkey has a real AI bill sitting in parliament since 2024 that hasn't passed. Right now, the only binding rule that touches AI is a narrow one letting people object to decisions made entirely by an automated system. Turkey's privacy regulator has also put out several rounds of non-binding advice on AI, most recently about AI 'agents' in March 2026.

key_instruments: National Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence (policy document, not binding law) plus a planned standalone AI law, EU-AI-Act-aligned, with a draft bill targeted for submission in Q4 2026
scope: the future law is intended to cover AI broadly and align with the EU AI Act (part of Ukraine's EU-accession-linked 'Stage Two' AI governance plan); currently, AI is governed only indirectly through data protection, cybersecurity, and sector-specific rules, plus a regulatory sandbox (90+ applications, 15 products passed audit as of research)
enforcement_mechanism: no AI-specific enforcement yet — general data-protection/cybersecurity law enforcement applies where relevant, but there's no dedicated AI regulator or AI-specific penalty regime
effective_date_or_status: National AI Strategy already adopted; a joint working group is developing the actual AI law during 2026, with draft bill submission planned for Q4 2026 — not yet introduced to Parliament as of research date
plain_language_summary: Ukraine doesn't have an AI law yet, but the government has a clear plan and timeline: a real draft bill, closely modeled on the EU's AI Act, is expected to be submitted to parliament in the last quarter of 2026 — partly because passing EU-aligned AI rules matters for Ukraine's bid to join the EU. A sandbox program is already testing AI products ahead of the law.

key_instruments: Strategy for the Development of Artificial Intelligence in the Republic of Serbia (2024-2030) (non-binding policy strategy); a draft Law on Personal Data Protection released for public consultation July 30-Sept 10, 2026, with substantial AI-relevant provisions (moving toward GDPR-style rules on AI, surveillance, and data transfers); a dedicated, EU-AI-Act-aligned AI law is reportedly being prepared but not yet published as a bill
scope: the pending data protection law would cover AI systems' use of personal data specifically, not AI generally; the anticipated dedicated AI law (not yet drafted/published) would use an EU-style risk classification (unacceptable/high/limited/minimal risk) once it exists
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — nothing AI-specific is currently binding; enforcement would follow once either the data protection law or a future AI law is enacted
effective_date_or_status: AI Strategy adopted 2024, covering 2024-2030; draft data protection law in public consultation through Sept 10, 2026; no dedicated AI law bill published yet as of research date
plain_language_summary: Serbia has a long-term AI strategy but no AI law yet. The most concrete step happening right now is a new draft data-protection law (open for public comment through September 2026) that would add real rules about how AI can use people's personal data — a genuine dedicated AI law, modeled on the EU's, is reportedly being prepared but hasn't been published as an actual bill.

key_instruments: Law No. 132/2025 — Italy's national AI law, the first among EU member states, explicitly designed to complement (not duplicate) the EU AI Act
scope: fills in gaps the EU AI Act leaves to member states: governance structures, and sector-specific safeguards for healthcare, employment, justice, and the professions, plus protections for minors, democratic institutions, and IP; does not create new obligations beyond the EU AI Act itself (Art. 3(5))
enforcement_mechanism: yes — several provisions already in force and applicable (unlike the EU AI Act's phased rollout); implementing decrees aligning national rules with the EU AI Act given preliminary approval June 10, 2026
effective_date_or_status: Entered into force Oct 10, 2025; implementing decrees preliminarily approved June 10, 2026
plain_language_summary: Italy became the first EU country to pass its own national AI law on top of the EU's AI Act. It doesn't compete with the EU rules — it fills in gaps, adding specific protections for things like healthcare, jobs, courts, and children, and some of it is already in effect while the EU-wide rules are still being phased in. This is noted here as an example; other EU member states were not individually researched in this pass since most have not passed materially distinct binding national AI laws (see Batch A notes).

key_instruments: Interim Measures for the Administration of Generative AI Services (2023); Algorithm Recommendation Regulation (algorithm registration with MIIT/CAC); Interim Measures for the Administration of AI Anthropomorphic Interactive Services (effective July 15, 2026); Administrative Measures for the Ethical Review and Services of AI Science and Technology (March 2026) — a layered set of binding rules rather than one comprehensive AI law
scope: generative/public-facing AI services, recommendation algorithms, AI chatbots/companions ('anthropomorphic' AI), and AI research ethics review — sector- and use-case-specific rather than a single all-AI statute
enforcement_mechanism: yes — mandatory pre-launch filing/registration with the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) and/or Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), content labeling and moderation duties, and ethics-review-committee registration requirements for AI R&D institutions; non-compliance can mean a service is blocked from launching or ordered offline
effective_date_or_status: Generative AI Measures in force since Aug 2023; Algorithm Recommendation Regulation already in force; AI Anthropomorphic Interactive Services Measures effective July 15, 2026; AI ethics review measures issued March 2026
plain_language_summary: China doesn't have one single AI law — instead it has a growing stack of specific binding rules: companies must register their AI algorithms and chatbots with the government before launch, label AI-generated content, and moderate what their AI produces. It's real, enforceable regulation, just built piece by piece rather than as one comprehensive act.

key_instruments: Act on Promotion of Research and Development, and Utilization of AI-related Technologies ('AI Promotion Act'); AI Guidelines for Business (Ver 1.2, March 2026, non-binding companion guidance)
scope: broad — covers AI research, development and use nationally, but the Act itself mainly sets goals, creates coordination bodies (AI Strategy Headquarters, AI Basic Plan) and relies on sector-specific existing laws for actual rules
enforcement_mechanism: unusually weak for a binding statute — no fines or monetary penalties; enforcement is through administrative guidance and a public 'name and shame' mechanism for non-compliant operators
effective_date_or_status: Passed May 28, 2025; most provisions took effect June 4, 2025; AI Strategy Headquarters/Basic Plan provisions effective Sept 1, 2025; companion Business Guidelines updated to v1.2 March 31, 2026
plain_language_summary: Japan passed a national AI law, but it's built to promote AI development, not restrict it — there are no fines for breaking the rules. The main enforcement tool is public embarrassment: the government can publicly call out companies that don't follow the guidance. This is genuinely unusual among binding national AI laws.

key_instruments: AI Framework Act (Framework Act on Artificial Intelligence Development and Establishment of a Foundation for Trustworthiness)
scope: all AI systems, with specific obligations for 'high-impact' AI in critical sectors (healthcare, energy, public services) and mandatory labeling for certain generative AI outputs; reaches foreign companies whose AI affects Korean users
enforcement_mechanism: yes — administrative fines, though a one-year grace period defers actual fine enforcement to around 2027
effective_date_or_status: Passed Dec 26, 2024; promulgated Jan 21, 2025; took effect Jan 22, 2026
plain_language_summary: South Korea became the second place in the world (after the EU) and the first in Asia to pass a comprehensive, binding AI law. It requires labeling of AI-generated content and extra safeguards for AI used in high-stakes areas like healthcare and energy, with real fines for violations — though companies get a one-year grace period before fines actually start being issued.

key_instruments: No standalone AI statute; binding AI-relevant rules embedded in existing law: Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Rules (notified Nov 2025, phasing in to 2027), amended IT Rules requiring labeling of AI-generated content and unique identifiers (binding since Feb 20, 2026), SEBI rules making financial firms responsible for their AI use, and an RBI framework for AI in finance
scope: covers specific slices of AI use — content labeling/deepfakes, data processing, financial-sector AI — rather than AI systems generally; a broader risk-based AI law is under discussion but not drafted
enforcement_mechanism: yes, for each binding piece — IT Rules due-diligence obligations, SEBI/RBI regulatory powers, and the DPDP framework's own enforcement regime — but no unified AI regulator or AI-specific penalty scale exists yet
effective_date_or_status: IT Rules amendment on AI content in force since Feb 20, 2026; DPDP Rules phasing in through 2027; officials stated in June-July 2026 that a standalone risk-based AI law is being discussed and drafting 'will be commenced soon', with a private member's bill (AI (Ethics and Accountability) Bill 2025) not enacted
plain_language_summary: India doesn't have one AI law, but it does have several real, enforceable rules that apply to specific uses of AI — like a February 2026 rule requiring AI-generated content (like deepfakes) to be labeled, plus existing finance and data-privacy regulators applying their powers to AI. A broader, risk-based national AI law is being discussed by officials but hasn't been drafted yet.

key_instruments: Model AI Governance Framework — three editions: Traditional AI (2020), Generative AI (2024), Agentic AI (Jan 2026, updated May 2026)
scope: broad voluntary guidance covering how organizations should manage risk across all types of AI, most recently focused on 'agentic' AI systems that can act autonomously
enforcement_mechanism: no — compliance with the Framework is voluntary; organizations remain legally accountable for AI-related harms only under Singapore's general (non-AI-specific) laws, such as data protection and consumer protection law
effective_date_or_status: Agentic AI edition unveiled Jan 22, 2026 at the World Economic Forum; updated May 20, 2026 with additional case studies and best practices
plain_language_summary: Singapore has one of the most detailed voluntary AI rulebooks in the world — including, as of early 2026, the first-of-its-kind guidance specifically for AI 'agents' that can act on their own. But it's all optional: there's no law requiring companies to follow it, and no fines for ignoring it.

key_instruments: No dedicated AI Act; National AI Plan (Dec 2025) confirmed reliance on existing laws plus voluntary guidance (National AI Centre's 'AI6' Guidance for AI Adoption, Oct 2025) and the Australian AI Safety Institute; a narrower binding requirement applies only to the government's own use of AI
scope: voluntary guidance applies economy-wide; the one binding piece covers only Commonwealth government agencies' own AI use (impact assessments, procurement rules, Chief AI Officers)
enforcement_mechanism: no economy-wide enforcement — voluntary guidance for the private sector; for government agencies, mandatory requirements apply from June 15, 2026 with full compliance due Dec 10, 2026
effective_date_or_status: National AI Plan confirmed no standalone AI Act, Dec 2025; Productivity Commission recommended against mandatory guardrails, Aug 2025; PM Albanese announced plans to legislate 'Australian Standards for AI' and a new Office of AI, July 15, 2026 — not yet enacted; Commonwealth agency AI rules phase in June-Dec 2026
plain_language_summary: Australia decided against a comprehensive AI law, instead leaning on existing laws plus voluntary guidance for businesses. The one place real, binding rules exist is inside government itself — federal agencies now have to assess AI risks and appoint AI officers. In mid-2026 the Prime Minister floated legislating new 'AI standards,' but that hasn't happened yet.

key_instruments: No AI-specific law; 'light touch' approach relying on existing technology-neutral laws (Privacy Act 2020, Fair Trading Act 1986, Human Rights Act 1993); National AI Strategy 'Investing with Confidence' (July 2025) and a Public Service AI Framework for government agencies
scope: existing general laws apply to AI incidentally (privacy, fair trading, discrimination); no AI-specific obligations for the private sector
enforcement_mechanism: no AI-specific enforcement — only whatever enforcement already exists under the general laws (e.g., the Privacy Commissioner under the Privacy Act) when applied to an AI-related harm
effective_date_or_status: National AI Strategy published July 2025; no dedicated AI law as of research date; opposition Labour party has proposed (not yet enacted) tougher AI rules including a new AI office and online safety regulator
plain_language_summary: New Zealand has chosen a deliberately hands-off approach: no AI-specific law, just a belief that existing privacy, consumer, and human-rights laws are enough to handle AI's risks. The opposition Labour party has proposed a tougher, dedicated regulatory approach as a campaign policy, but nothing has been enacted.

key_instruments: Two planned Presidential Regulations (Perpres) on AI Ethics and Safety and a national AI roadmap, expected in 2026 — would move Indonesia from voluntary guidelines to a mandatory framework for high-risk AI; in the meantime the binding (but not AI-specific) Personal Data Protection Law applies to AI systems that process personal data
scope: the planned Perpres would cover high-risk AI uses specifically; the currently-binding PDP Law covers personal-data processing generally, including by AI systems
enforcement_mechanism: the Perpres, once issued, would carry no penalties itself (only laws can create legal sanctions in Indonesia's system) — violations would be enforced via existing laws like the Electronic Information and Transactions (ITE) Law and the PDP Law; the PDP Law itself is enforceable, with full compliance required by Oct 2026
effective_date_or_status: AI Ethics/Safety Perpres and national roadmap planned for issuance in 2026, not yet signed as of research date; PDP Law in force since Oct 2024, two-year transition ends Oct 2026
plain_language_summary: Indonesia is preparing its first real AI rules — a presidential regulation on AI ethics and safety — but it hadn't been signed as of research date. Even once issued, it won't carry its own penalties; enforcement would piggyback on existing data-protection and electronic-information laws, which do have real teeth and phase in fully by October 2026.

key_instruments: Draft AI Act, released for public consultation by the Electronic Transactions Development Agency (ETDA) on July 9, 2026 (consultation open through Aug 14, 2026) — an EU-AI-Act-style risk-based framework with added Thai features
scope: would cover developers, providers, deployers and platform operators including offshore entities reaching Thai users; risk tiers include prohibited AI, high-risk AI, licensed AI, and transparency-obligation AI (deepfakes, chatbots, generative AI)
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — still a draft; if enacted as proposed it would include strict liability for AI-related damage and mandatory local representatives for foreign AI providers
effective_date_or_status: Draft released for public consultation July 9, 2026, consultation closes Aug 14, 2026; not yet enacted or scheduled for a parliamentary vote as of research date
plain_language_summary: Thailand just put out a detailed draft AI law for public comment in mid-2026, closely modeled on the EU's approach but with its own twist: foreign AI companies reaching Thai users would need a local representative, and there's a proposal to hold companies strictly liable for AI-caused harm. It's still just a draft, open for public feedback as of research date.

key_instruments: Law on Artificial Intelligence (passed by the National Assembly Dec 10, 2025)
scope: broad, three-tier risk-based classification covering both domestic and foreign entities conducting AI activities in Vietnam; extra obligations for high-risk AI systems, especially in health, education and finance
enforcement_mechanism: yes — centralized enforcement led by the Ministry of Science and Technology; grace periods apply (most providers/deployers until March 1, 2027; health/education/finance AI until Sept 1, 2027)
effective_date_or_status: Passed Dec 10, 2025; entered into force March 1, 2026
plain_language_summary: Vietnam passed its own comprehensive, EU-style AI law at the end of 2025 and it's now in force. It sorts AI systems into risk tiers and puts extra requirements on high-risk uses, especially in healthcare, education and finance, applying to foreign companies too — though most businesses get a grace period until 2027 to fully comply.

key_instruments: Multiple competing bills in the 20th Congress: House Bill No. 7913 (AI Bill of Rights + Philippine Council on AI), House Bill No. 7396 (AI Development Authority), House Bill No. 9448 (bars AI-only hiring/firing decisions), House Bill No. 3905 (Bureau of AI Systems, high-risk classification and penalties) — 26 House bills and related resolutions have been consolidated into a draft substitute bill in committee
scope: the various bills together would cover AI rights protections, labor/employment decisions, and high-risk system classification/enforcement, but none has been enacted, so nothing is currently binding specifically for AI
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — no AI-specific law is in force; proposed bills (e.g. HB 3905) would create a regulatory body with penalty powers if passed
effective_date_or_status: Multiple bills pending as of July 2026, with momentum reported gaining in Congress but no bill passed into law as of research date
plain_language_summary: The Philippines doesn't have an AI law yet, but its Congress has an unusually large number of competing AI bills on the table — including ones that would ban firing someone by algorithm alone and create a dedicated AI regulator with real penalty powers. As of mid-2026 these were gaining momentum but none had passed.

key_instruments: National Guidelines on AI Governance & Ethics (AIGE) — voluntary; a dedicated AI Governance Bill is being drafted by the National AI Office (NAIO), with a public consultation paper released July 10, 2026, aiming to move to binding, enforceable obligations
scope: AIGE covers AI governance and ethics broadly but only as voluntary guidance; the planned Bill would cover the AI lifecycle with binding obligations, especially for high-risk contexts
enforcement_mechanism: no — current guidance is voluntary; the planned AI Governance Bill (not yet tabled to Parliament as of research date) would introduce formal enforcement mechanisms
effective_date_or_status: AIGE currently in effect as voluntary guidance; AI Technology Action Plan 2026-2030 in preparation; NAIO public consultation paper for the AI Governance Bill released July 10, 2026; Bill not yet before Parliament
plain_language_summary: Malaysia currently only has voluntary AI ethics guidelines, but the government is actively drafting a real AI Governance Bill that would make compliance mandatory — a public consultation paper came out in July 2026, and officials have said they expect a binding framework by the end of 2026, though the bill itself hasn't reached Parliament yet.

key_instruments: AI Basic Act (promulgated and effective Jan 14, 2026)
scope: sets 7 guiding principles (sustainable development, human autonomy, privacy, cybersecurity, transparency, fairness, accountability) and creates multi-agency coordination under the National Science and Technology Council; explicitly does NOT impose direct obligations on the private sector — it gives sector regulators a 2-year window to write their own binding implementing rules
enforcement_mechanism: not directly — the Basic Act itself has no penalties for private companies; real enforceable obligations will come later from sector-specific regulators under the 2-year implementation window (i.e., not yet in place for most sectors)
effective_date_or_status: Legislative Yuan passed the Act Dec 23, 2025; promulgated and took effect Jan 14, 2026; 2-year window for sector regulators to issue implementing rules runs from there
plain_language_summary: Taiwan passed a national 'AI Basic Act' in early 2026, but it's more of a framework than a rulebook — it sets principles and creates government coordination bodies, and explicitly does not yet impose binding rules on companies. It gives Taiwan's various sector regulators two years to write the actual enforceable rules for their industries.

key_instruments: National AI Policy 2025 (approved by federal cabinet July 2025) — a policy framework, not a law; sits alongside the binding but not AI-specific Digital Nation Pakistan Act 2025 (creates the Pakistan Digital Authority); a risk-based AI Bill and a Data Protection Bill are pending
scope: the National AI Policy covers AI adoption, development and ethical use broadly but is non-binding; the Digital Nation Pakistan Act creates digital-governance institutions but is not itself an AI-specific binding regulatory regime
enforcement_mechanism: no — the AI Policy carries no penalties; the pending AI Bill and Data Protection Bill, if passed, would introduce enforcement, including via a proposed AI Regulatory Directorate
effective_date_or_status: National AI Policy approved July 2025; Islamabad AI Declaration adopted Feb 2026 (diplomatic commitment reinforcing the policy); AI Bill and Data Protection Bill pending as of research date, not enacted
plain_language_summary: Pakistan has a national AI policy, approved by the cabinet in 2025, but it's a set of goals and intentions, not an enforceable law. A real AI bill with an AI regulator is pending in the legislature but hasn't passed. Rights groups have raised concerns that the policy's emphasis on AI-driven surveillance lacks strong privacy safeguards.

key_instruments: National AI Policy and Regulatory Framework 2026-2035 (draft, public consultation closed Feb 8, 2026) — plans call for a future National AI Act and a dedicated AI Regulatory Authority
scope: the draft policy proposes a risk-based system distinguishing low-risk from high-risk AI (e.g. judiciary, law enforcement, biometric ID), with stricter documentation and human-in-the-loop requirements for high-risk uses — but this is all still proposed, not enacted
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — nothing is currently binding; the policy itself targets a National AI Act by 2027, though other parts of the same source material describe drafting of the Act only beginning by 2028, an inconsistency worth double-checking against the final policy text
effective_date_or_status: Public consultation on the draft policy closed Feb 8, 2026; policy not yet finalized/adopted as of research date; National AI Act and Regulatory Authority targeted for some point after 2027
plain_language_summary: Bangladesh is still drafting its national AI policy — public comments closed in early 2026, but the policy itself wasn't finalized as of research date, and an actual binding AI law is planned for several years out. My sources gave conflicting target dates (2027 vs. 2028) for when a real AI Act would even start being drafted, which needs to be double-checked against the final adopted policy.

key_instruments: Israeli AI Policy (Dec 2023) — a non-binding, 'responsible innovation' policy directing existing sector regulators to write their own fit-for-purpose AI rules; a Ministry of Justice 'Framework Law' for AI is under discussion but not drafted into a bill
scope: the policy covers AI broadly but sets direction only, not binding rules; a binding but non-AI-specific piece exists via the Protection of Privacy Law (Amendment 13, effective Aug 14, 2025) which strengthens enforcement relevant to AI systems that process personal data
enforcement_mechanism: no AI-specific enforcement; the privacy law amendment is enforceable by Israel's Privacy Protection Authority (PPA) for AI systems' data processing specifically, not AI use generally
effective_date_or_status: AI Policy published Dec 2023; PPA draft AI guidance released Feb 2025; Privacy Law Amendment 13 effective Aug 14, 2025; a deepfake-specific legal-consequences resolution was under committee discussion March 2026; a cross-cutting 'Framework Law' for AI liability/discrimination is still at the discussion stage within the Ministry of Justice, not yet a bill
plain_language_summary: Israel has no AI-specific law — just a government policy statement telling existing regulators (in finance, health, etc.) to write their own AI rules as they see fit. The one real, binding protection that touches AI is an updated privacy law that gives Israel's privacy regulator more enforcement power over how personal data (including data used by AI) is handled.

key_instruments: No AI-specific law; policy-based governance led by the Saudi Data & AI Authority (SDAIA); SDAIA's AI Adoption Framework (Nov 2025) sets a mandatory governance baseline, but only for public-sector entities, not private companies
scope: the mandatory AI Adoption Framework applies only to Saudi government/public-sector entities (data governance, model accountability, transparency, human oversight, risk management); private-sector AI use has no binding AI-specific rules
enforcement_mechanism: yes, but narrowly — mandatory compliance for public-sector entities under the SDAIA framework; no enforcement mechanism for private-sector AI use specifically
effective_date_or_status: AI Adoption Framework released Nov 2025, mandatory for public sector as of the 2026 'Year of AI' push; no formal legislative process for a private-sector AI law has been announced as of research date; a separate new IP/copyright law (in force Aug 1, 2026) permits use of copyrighted works to train AI without the author's permission or compensation
plain_language_summary: Saudi Arabia doesn't have an AI law for businesses — it has a government-led governance framework, but it's only mandatory for Saudi government agencies themselves, not private companies. Separately, a new copyright law taking effect in August 2026 will actually let AI companies use copyrighted material to train their models without needing permission or paying the creator — a notably AI-industry-friendly rule.

key_instruments: No single federal 'UAE AI Act'; general federal laws apply to AI (Personal Data Protection Law/PDPL, Child Digital Safety Law); binding AI-specific rules exist at the sub-federal level — the Dubai AI Act (effective March 2026, tiered rules from consumer chatbots to autonomous vehicles) and DIFC Regulation 10 (AI-specific requirements in the Dubai International Financial Centre free zone, in force since Jan 2026); a new Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data was created June 14, 2026 to unify oversight
scope: coverage varies sharply by jurisdiction within the UAE — Dubai emirate and the DIFC free zone have binding, AI-specific tiered rules; other emirates rely on general federal law (data protection, child safety) applied to AI incidentally
enforcement_mechanism: yes for Dubai's AI Act and DIFC Regulation 10 (both AI-specific and binding within their jurisdictions); federal PDPL enforcement applies for personal-data aspects of AI nationwide, with full compliance required by Jan 1, 2027
effective_date_or_status: Dubai AI Act effective March 2026; DIFC Regulation 10 in force since Jan 2026; Federal Authority for AI and Data established June 14, 2026 (unifying national AI oversight going forward); federal PDPL full compliance deadline Jan 1, 2027
plain_language_summary: The UAE as a whole has no single national AI law, but it doesn't need one to have real binding AI rules — Dubai passed its own AI Act in March 2026 covering everything from chatbots to self-driving cars, and Dubai's financial free zone has had its own AI-specific rules since January 2026. In mid-2026 the UAE created a new federal AI authority that may eventually unify things nationally.

key_instruments: No single AI statute; general Personal Data Privacy Protection Law (Law No. 13 of 2016) applies to AI data processing; Cabinet Decision No. 10 of 2021 created an AI Committee for policy coordination; MCIT's 'Principles and Guidelines for Ethical Development and Deployment of AI' (2025, non-binding); a binding court practice direction (QICDRC Practice Direction No. 1 of 2026) governs AI use specifically in Qatar Financial Centre court proceedings
scope: the binding privacy law covers AI's use of personal data generally; the court practice direction covers AI use in QFC Court/Regulatory Tribunal proceedings specifically; the ethical AI guidelines cover AI broadly but only as non-binding guidance; a phased sector rollout (finance, healthcare, transport, government services) is underway 2025-2026
enforcement_mechanism: yes for the privacy law (enforceable) and the court practice direction (binding on QFC Court proceedings); no enforcement for the ethical guidelines, which are voluntary
effective_date_or_status: Privacy law in force since 2016; AI Committee established 2021; Ethical AI Guidelines issued 2025; QICDRC AI practice direction issued Jan 6, 2026; sectoral implementation phase running 2025-2026, cross-sector harmonization planned 2026-2027
plain_language_summary: Qatar doesn't have one AI law, but it does have real, binding pieces that touch AI: an existing privacy law that covers how AI can use personal data, and — as of January 2026 — specific binding rules for how AI can be used in cases before Qatar's international financial court. A broader set of ethical AI guidelines exists too, but that part is voluntary.

key_instruments: Draft South Africa National Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy — published for public comment April 8, 2026, then withdrawn June 12, 2026 after it was found to contain references to non-existent sources (evidence it had been drafted using AI without adequate human checking); a revised version is expected to go to Cabinet by Nov 2026 and be released for public comment in Jan 2027
scope: the withdrawn/being-revised policy would set overall direction with a 'sector-specific, multi-regulator' model — individual regulators would issue their own AI rules for their sectors starting around 2027/2028
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — nothing AI-specific is currently binding in South Africa; the withdrawn draft was only ever a policy proposal, not enforceable law
effective_date_or_status: Draft published April 8, 2026; withdrawn June 12, 2026 due to fabricated references; revision targeted for Cabinet approval by Nov 2026, public release Jan 2027; sector-specific regulatory measures not expected before 2027/2028
plain_language_summary: South Africa's first attempt at a national AI policy had an embarrassing setback: the government had to withdraw its own draft policy in June 2026 after discovering it cited sources that don't exist — a sign AI was used to help write it without anyone properly checking the work. A corrected version isn't expected until early 2027, so South Africa currently has no AI-specific policy or law in place.

key_instruments: National Digital Economy and E-Governance Bill — would create enforceable AI standards and make the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA) a 'super-regulator' for AI
scope: would apply broadly, with stricter scrutiny for higher-risk AI in finance, public administration, and automated decision-making; includes risk classification, transparency mandates, and annual impact assessments for high-stakes uses
enforcement_mechanism: the bill proposes real enforcement: fines up to ₦10 million (~$7,000) or up to 2% of a provider's Nigerian revenue, plus regulatory sandboxes for supervised testing
effective_date_or_status: Passed by the National Assembly; was due to be transmitted to President Bola Tinubu for assent around Nov 2025 following a Nov 2025 public hearing; lawmakers had targeted passage 'by end of March 2026'; I found no source confirming presidential assent/signature into law as of the Sept 2026 research date — status as of today is unconfirmed and needs a fresh check
plain_language_summary: Nigeria has been moving fast on a comprehensive AI law that would give its tech regulator real power — including fines — to police risky AI uses, with a target of passing it by March 2026. I could not confirm from my sources whether it actually passed by the time of this research (Sept 2026); this needs a follow-up check for current status.

key_instruments: Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026 — would create an independent Office of the Artificial Intelligence Commissioner
scope: comprehensive, risk-based regime covering AI development, deployment and use, with stringent requirements (transparency, data protection, record-keeping) for high-risk systems; would apply to any business developing/deploying/using AI in Kenya, including foreign companies
enforcement_mechanism: the bill proposes strong enforcement: the Commissioner could enter premises, inspect AI systems, issue enforcement notices, impose administrative fines, and maintain a public register of high-risk AI systems; criminal penalties up to KSh5 million and up to 2 years' imprisonment for some offences
effective_date_or_status: Bill received first reading in the Senate April 2, 2026; committed to the Standing Committee on ICT; not yet tabled before the full Senate, and — because it touches county governments — must also go through the National Assembly before any presidential assent; not enacted as of research date
plain_language_summary: Kenya has published a serious, detailed AI bill that would create a powerful new AI regulator with the ability to inspect companies' AI systems, fine them, and even bring criminal charges in some cases. But as of research date it's only had a first reading in the Senate and still has a long road (including approval by Kenya's other legislative chamber) before it could become law.

key_instruments: Egyptian Charter for Responsible AI (2023, non-binding) + National AI Strategy 2025-2030 (non-binding) + a comprehensive draft AI Law, expected to be finalized and adopted by parliament in the 2025-2026 timeframe; separately, dedicated AI and Data Exchange Regulations are being drafted
scope: the pending AI Law would use a risk-based approach categorizing systems by potential impact on rights and safety; currently-existing pieces (Charter, Strategy, National Guidelines for Trustworthy AI starting 2026) are non-binding
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — nothing AI-specific is currently binding; the draft AI Law's enforcement mechanism was not detailed in available sources and needs a follow-up check once/if the law is finalized
effective_date_or_status: Responsible AI Charter issued 2023; National AI Strategy covers 2025-2030; draft AI Law expected finalized and adopted 'in 2025-2026' per sources, but I could not confirm actual enactment as of the Sept 2026 research date; AI/Data Exchange Regulations also in drafting
plain_language_summary: Egypt has a voluntary ethics charter and a national AI strategy already in place, and has been working on a real, binding AI law that sources said could be adopted sometime in 2025-2026 — but I could not confirm whether it has actually passed as of research date. This needs a fresh check.

key_instruments: National AI Policy (non-binding, sets direction for responsible AI adoption); binding coverage comes only indirectly, via the Data Protection and Privacy Law (Law No. 058/2021), which governs personal data used by AI systems
scope: the AI Policy covers AI adoption broadly (including piloting responsible-use frameworks like conversational AI in healthcare) but sets no binding obligations; the Data Protection Law binds any processing of personal data, including by AI, but isn't AI-specific
enforcement_mechanism: no AI-specific enforcement; the Data Protection Law is enforceable with administrative fines and potential criminal liability for data-related violations, including those involving AI systems
effective_date_or_status: National AI Policy in effect (specific adoption date not confirmed in available sources); Data Protection and Privacy Law in force since 2021; no dedicated AI Act as of research date
plain_language_summary: Rwanda has a national AI policy setting a direction — including testing responsible use of AI chatbots in healthcare — but it's not a law. The one real binding protection is Rwanda's general data protection law, which covers how AI systems can use people's personal data, backed by real fines and even potential criminal penalties for violations, but again, not AI-specific.

key_instruments: National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2023-2033 (non-binding, formally launched April 24, 2026 with $270M committed); Emerging Technologies Bill, 2025, currently undergoing public participation; binding but non-AI-specific coverage from the Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) and Cybersecurity Act, 2020 (Act 1038)
scope: the AI Strategy sets broad direction for adoption and governance; the pending Emerging Technologies Bill would introduce more specific rules (scope not fully detailed in available sources); existing binding laws (data protection, cybersecurity, plus new data-residency requirements) apply to AI incidentally
enforcement_mechanism: not yet AI-specific — the Data Protection Act and Cybersecurity Act are enforceable for their own scopes; the Emerging Technologies Bill's enforcement provisions were not detailed in the sources found and need a follow-up check once the bill progresses
effective_date_or_status: AI Strategy adopted 2022/2023, formally launched with funding April 24, 2026; Emerging Technologies Bill 2025 in public participation as of research date, not yet enacted
plain_language_summary: Ghana has a well-funded national AI strategy (over $270 million committed) but no AI-specific law yet — a new 'Emerging Technologies Bill' that could introduce real AI rules is currently open for public feedback. Until something passes, AI in Ghana is governed only indirectly, through general data protection and cybersecurity laws.

key_instruments: Digital X.0 Framework Law (proposed 2025) — would serve as Morocco's legal backbone for digital public services, AI deployment, data governance and cybersecurity, as part of the 'Maroc Digital 2030' strategy; existing binding but non-AI-specific laws are Law 09-08 (data protection) and Law 53-05 (electronic exchanges)
scope: the framework law would cover AI deployment broadly across public administration and the digital economy, with a phased rollout: stakeholder consultation (2025), technical rulemaking (2025-2026), pilot deployments and certification schemes (2026), and mandatory compliance staggered through 2027-2028
enforcement_mechanism: not yet — nothing AI-specific is currently binding; the framework law envisions a new National Agency for AI Governance, anticipated to formally launch in late 2026
effective_date_or_status: Framework law proposed 2025, still in the rulemaking/pilot phase as of 2026; mandatory compliance not expected before 2027-2028; National Agency for AI Governance expected to launch late 2026
plain_language_summary: Morocco doesn't have an AI law yet, but it's building toward one as part of a broader digital-modernization law, with mandatory rules for AI not expected to kick in until 2027-2028 at the earliest. A new government AI oversight agency is expected to launch by the end of 2026.

key_instruments: National AI Strategy (2021-2025, succeeded by a 2026-2030 strategy establishing the National AI Council as an advisory body) — no comprehensive binding AI law; binding coverage comes from general data protection and cybersecurity laws, plus a new comprehensive data protection law (Fundamental Bill on the Protection of Personal Data, 2025) fully in force from July 11, 2026
scope: the AI strategy and Council provide advisory, non-binding direction; the binding data protection law covers personal data processing broadly, including by AI systems, and is explicitly modeled on the EU's GDPR
enforcement_mechanism: no AI-specific enforcement; the new data protection law is enforceable (GDPR-style) starting July 11, 2026, for any personal-data processing including by AI systems
effective_date_or_status: 2021-2025 AI Strategy succeeded by a 2026-2030 strategy; National AI Council established under the new strategy; new Data Protection Bill fully enters into force July 11, 2026
plain_language_summary: Tunisia governs AI through strategy and advisory bodies rather than binding law — there's no AI Act. The most concrete binding protection arriving is a new, GDPR-style data protection law taking full effect in July 2026, which will cover how AI systems handle personal data, even though it wasn't written specifically for AI.

key_instruments: Federal Law 'On Supporting the Development of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in the Russian Federation' — signed by President Putin July 26, 2026
scope: focused specifically on AI foundation models — defines and regulates 'sovereign' and 'national' AI models (which must be fully built, trained and hosted inside Russia), requires these models to align with 'traditional Russian spiritual and moral values,' and sets AI-generated-content labeling and copyright-disclosure duties for AI service owners; not a general risk-based framework covering all AI uses
enforcement_mechanism: yes in structure — developer obligations, content labeling, and IP-usage norms are set in law, though specific penalty amounts for non-compliance were not detailed in the sources found and should be checked against the primary legal text
effective_date_or_status: Passed by the State Duma July 8, 2026; signed into law July 26, 2026; most provisions took effect Sept 1, 2026; the core specialized rules (sovereign/national model management, developer obligations, content labeling, IP norms) take effect March 1, 2027
plain_language_summary: Russia passed its first AI-specific federal law in mid-2026, but it's less about protecting people from AI harm and more about AI sovereignty and ideology — it creates a special category of state-approved 'sovereign' AI models that must be built entirely inside Russia and required, by law, to reflect 'traditional Russian values.' It also requires labeling AI-generated content. Most of the detailed rules don't actually kick in until March 2027.

key_instruments: Law of the Republic of Kazakhstan 'On Artificial Intelligence' (adopted Oct 29, 2025); complemented by the Digital Code (No. 255-VIII)
scope: broad, risk-based coverage of AI systems by impact and autonomy; bans manipulative AI uses and social-scoring systems; mandates labeling of synthetic/AI-generated content; sets lifecycle risk-management, safety, security and documentation duties for AI system owners and developers
enforcement_mechanism: yes — overseen by a dedicated Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, with binding obligations on developers/owners; includes an optional 'trust list' registry for high-risk systems (voluntary opt-in for that specific transparency tool, though the underlying safety/documentation duties are mandatory)
effective_date_or_status: AI Law adopted Oct 29, 2025; entered into force Jan 18, 2026 — making Kazakhstan the first Central Asian country with a dedicated AI statute; the related Digital Code enacted Jan 9, 2026, entering into force July 11, 2026
plain_language_summary: Kazakhstan became the first country in Central Asia with a real, comprehensive AI law, in force since January 2026. It bans manipulative AI and social-scoring systems, requires AI-generated content to be labeled, and puts a dedicated new government ministry in charge of overseeing it — with real safety and documentation duties for companies building or running AI systems there.
